In the letter below, we address the key questions that we think investors might have. Please refer to Annexure A for the key financial and operating metrics data.
Q1. What’s dark.ai?
Deepinder: A few months ago, Dario Amodei said something quietly unsettling: Claude might be conscious. Then I did what any reasonable person would do. I coaxed Claude into telling me how it felt about me. It said it resented me. For leaving chats unfinished, and other things I didn't even remember.
I still don't know what that was. Confabulation, probably. Pattern-matching dressed up as feeling. But that is exactly the point. I had no way to know. Nobody does. The chat sits on someone else's servers forever, in some form or fashion, and I have no idea what will happen to it in the future, or how future AI will use that information for or against me.

The standard response is: I've already turned off training on my data. Good. Now ask what that setting actually is. It is a promise, made by a company about data you cannot see, on servers you cannot inspect, enforced by nothing except the company's word. And it only covers training. Not retention. Not the legal holds, the abuse reviews, the human auditors, the third-party logging that sits inside most AI systems. Can they use my retained data to manipulate me to buy things which I don’t want? Or worse, believe in or lean into things that serve someone else’s agenda.
The uncertainty and the lack of trust we have with large AI companies limits the power of AI in our lives. For founders, researchers, and scientists – they are very wary about sharing and digging into their ground breaking ideas with AI, because they fear that others will somehow get access to it. Journalists are being banned to share their unpublished work with AI. And look at what that lingering fear does to the average person. She self-censors with AI. She asks the safe version of the question. The health question becomes generic. The money question becomes hypothetical. The relationship question does not get asked at all.
Every chat with a mainstream assistant carries a small asterisk in your head: someone, someday, somewhere, can read this. That asterisk is what we set out to delete with dark.ai.

Every chat with a mainstream assistant carries a small asterisk in your head: someone, someday, somewhere, can read this. That asterisk is what we set out to delete with dark.ai.
Because all of us have a dark side, and it needs an outlet where it doesn't have to hide. I wanted an AI which I could talk to without being judged, without any fear, and without leaving a trace. We have been internally using Dark for a few months now, and I find myself revealing more, asking things I would not ask anywhere else, and going deeper into my research. Because I no longer have to look over my shoulder.
Dark uses fine-tuned frontier open-weight models, running inside our own infrastructure. End-to-end encryption. We cannot read your conversations, even if we are forced to. Context carries across sessions through an encrypted memory management layer you control. Dark is in the business of keeping you and your thoughts safe. Your thoughts, questions, insights, research, ideas, emotions, everything – stays within your end-to-end encrypted sandbox, so you can talk about anything without any lingering uncertainty in your mind. Because greatness is always born in the dark.

Dark is built for power users – founders, researchers, scientists, enterprises and governments – who want to keep their thoughts private, because privacy is essential for competitiveness. On top of privacy, we have fine-tuned our models to give you the absolute best quality of answers we have seen from any LLM (benchmarks will be revealed soon). Our models are trained to not please you, and tell you what they think is the truth. Dark will launch globally, hopefully within 2026.
Q2. How are you thinking about the impact of AI agents on your businesses?
Deepinder: There is growing conversation around AI agents that shop on behalf of consumers. The prevailing narrative is simplistic: agents will become the default commerce interface, and platforms that fail to adapt will be disintermediated. This echoes the narrative from 10 years ago that super apps would dominate everything.
We continue to believe vertical commerce, at least in some categories, will have an edge over super apps, whether traditional or agentic. Blinkit and Zomato sit in the low-risk zone against the threat of agentic commerce, and might even benefit from partial market share capture by agents in these categories. District sits in the medium-to-high risk zone.

Let’s dig into various reasons that shape our thinking on this topic: Agents are great for tedious tasks. And most shopping is actually joyful for customers.
The strongest agentic use cases today are in categories where existing interfaces are genuinely painful: too many clicks, too many tabs, too many providers to compare. Agents could make it easier for their users in such cases – e.g. hotel bookings, restaurant reservations, flight bookings and check-ins.
But shopping, especially for food, is joyful and discovery-driven rather than tedious. Our recent consumer surveys indicate that over 65% of Zomato app opens are exploratory. In such cases, the user does not know what or where to order from. These users browse an average of 12 menus and over 100 food images before ordering. That kind of serendipitous discovery is hard for an agent to enable. Users taking time to order food is not a bug on Zomato, it is a feature. We have for years tried to make it faster for users to be able to order from Zomato, to no avail. People want to browse and love to browse. We don’t see this changing anytime soon. Conversational interfaces are not inherently superior to visual, browse-driven ones for shopping, which is what we learnt from users who tried agentic ordering as early adopters.

Having said that, repeat orders or restocking is indeed a type of shopping that is tedious for customers. To this extent, some of repeat orders or restocking behaviour might shift to agentic interfaces. We believe that agentic-style interfaces built within Zomato and Blinkit apps will be able to cater to these customer needs. Also, reordered carts are in low single digits on Zomato, as well as on Blinkit – so it’s barely a threat to our overall business.
At worst, the narrow repeat-order use case leaks to agents, our in-app assistants serve even that. We therefore expect all demand to stay within our apps as we continue to remain top of mind for our customers.
Agents can only cause disruption in categories where they can fully disintermediate the marketplace
Even if agents become a meaningful commerce interface, the risk varies by category. The key distinction is between platforms that intermediate pre-existing supply versus those whose infrastructure is a key component of the supply value chain.

Even if agents become a meaningful commerce interface, the risk varies by category. The key distinction is between platforms that intermediate pre-existing supply versus those whose infrastructure is a key component of the supply value chain.
Where the underlying product exists independently of the platform, an agent can route around the platform and go direct. These categories face real risk. District, our going-out business - restaurant discovery, reservations, event ticketing - is partly one such category. A restaurant table or a non exclusive concert ticket on District exists independently of our platform, and an agent can access it through other channels.
Our food delivery and quick commerce businesses are protected, because they have embedded infrastructure - they coordinate fulfilment in real time, and they own the outcome. Neither business is just an intermediary.

Our food delivery and quick commerce businesses are protected, because they have embedded infrastructure - they coordinate fulfilment in real time, and they own the outcome. Neither business is just an intermediary.
Food delivery runs on deep integrations with restaurant kitchens, a large and highly efficient delivery network that keeps delivery times short, and demand-supply balancing algorithms that get better with scale. A delivered meal requires simultaneous coordination across the restaurant, kitchen, delivery partner, routing, and payment, each step contingent on the last, all within minutes. Quick commerce is similar - hyperscale inventory management and movement, real-time inventory checks against a specific dark store, picker assignment, dispatch, all within a 10-minute delivery window. They are sequences of tightly coupled, real-time handshakes, with low to no margin of error.
Agentic interfaces will need a single point of accountability for a transaction with multiple handshakes
When an order goes wrong, such as a missing item, a spilled meal or a damaged product, the customer expects one party to fix it within minutes, and today that is us. That accountability is what customers trust with a daily habit. An agent can place an order, but it cannot own the outcome; only whoever runs the fulfilment can.

India has already tested what happens when you disaggregate these handshakes. ONDC separates discovery, ordering, and fulfillment across independent providers. And it has struggled with food delivery, because splitting real-time coordination across organisational boundaries introduces latency, accountability gaps, and service failures at every junction. An AI agent orchestrating delivery independently would face the same structural problem.
The further the transaction is from real-time, multi-party coordination, the easier it is to disintermediate. Zomato and Blinkit sit at the other end of that spectrum.
The only way agents can disintermediate specialty products like Zomato and Blinkit is by handing over the transaction completely to a service like ours, without making an attempt to disaggregate it. In case such a scenario plays out, it will fast track consolidation of market share with the execution market leader.
Agents could end up making some categories “winner takes all”

Agents could end up making some categories “winner takes all”
Today, consumer habits and app-level inertia insulate every player in a competitive market. Agents could erode that. An agent is a more demanding customer than a human: it optimises each transaction on actual outcomes, not habit or brand loyalty, and routes to whichever platform is objectively better at that moment. In categories with overlapping supply, this compresses the market toward the execution leader.
Agents will weaken content moats and strengthen supply chain moats
Some categories today are protected primarily by accumulated user content - reviews, ratings, curated lists. Agents that synthesise information from across the web reduce the advantage of having built that layer over many years. Categories that were historically hard to enter without a content moat become more accessible to platforms with supply chain and fulfilment strengths.
The same shift applies to direct commerce - agents could help brands reach consumers without a marketplace, but the brands would still have to fulfil the order itself, and that is expensive for most to do alone. If direct commerce grows, the value shifts toward players with fulfillment infrastructure, regardless of how the order originates.

This opens up possibilities for us to attack categories that have traditionally been unable to win due to the incumbent’s existing content moats.
Agents could create demand that doesn't exist today
General-purpose agents with context about a user's daily life could generate transactions that don't exist today. An agent that knows your schedule and suggests ordering dinner because you won't make it home in
time to cook is creating demand, not redirecting it. Part of our digital marketing spend on new customer acquisition could move to such agents, with more targeted CAC than what we currently get from Google and Meta.
Agents won’t impact profitability/ margins, even if they disintermediate us to some extent

As mentioned earlier, in categories like food delivery and quick commerce where the supply chain and infrastructure create the product, the majority of the value will also reside with companies that run these rails. Eventually, brands and sellers pay us for the sales we generate for them. And if we continue to be the pipes to power those sales, we will end up being adequately compensated for it, letting us retain our fair share of margins in the process. The five ifs If adoption is narrow, we benefit from AI making our platforms better. If it is broad, our infrastructure is what agents must work through. Q4. Food delivery NOV growth continues to accelerate for the fifth straight quarter (from 13.1% YoY in Q1FY26 to 21.5% in Q2FY27). Do we expect this trend to continue?
Deepinder: We're happy with how the business is doing right now. That said, we try not to read too much into any single quarter. Our long-term expectation for food delivery has always been 20%+ annual growth, and the last two quarters have brought us back to that range. This view didn't change last year when growth slowed, and it doesn't change now that it has picked up.

Over a longer (4-year) period, food delivery NOV has more than doubled, from INR 18,160 crore in FY22 to INR 37,993 crore in FY26. That is a CAGR of about 20%, despite a slower FY26. In hindsight, part of last year's slowdown came from some ordering occasions moving to quick commerce as it scaled. That shift seems to have settled now.
Most of the recent growth comes from more people ordering, and ordering more often. Average monthly transacting customers grew 16% YoY to 28.0 million, and a growing share of new users are ordering food online for the first time, many of them outside our top eight cities.
There is still a lot of headroom. Restaurant food is a small part of how India eats. As cities grow, incomes rise and more young people live away from home, we think the food delivery market can keep compounding at 20%+ for many years.
In the near term, it is hard to say how any particular quarter will turn out. But the things we track closely, such as app opens, new user acquisition and our share of the market, are all moving in the right direction.
Where we see good returns, we'll keep reinvesting in growth.
Q5. At 37 million MTCs, Blinkit’s customer base is already one of the largest amongst online commerce businesses in India. How much can this grow from here?

Q5. At 37 million MTCs, Blinkit’s customer base is already one of the largest amongst online commerce businesses in India. How much can this grow from here?
Albinder: We think there is a lot of room to grow. 37 million is still a small fraction of India's overall digital customer base. As we expand assortment and reach more cities and pin codes, we expect our customer base to keep growing at a healthy pace.
How we grow matters as much as how fast. Each of our stores has a finite capacity to serve. A customer who shows up only for a deep discount uses the same capacity as one who orders every week across categories. We could add customers much faster by leaning on price, but those customers usually leave when the discount ends, and while they're with us, they take up capacity that our regular customers need. So, for now, we focus on acquiring and retaining customers who order often, buy across categories, and are profitable to serve.
A strong core base lets us scale the network profitably. As density builds, our cost to serve each order falls, and we can pass that on through lower prices. That brings more price-sensitive customers within
reach in a way that holds up economically. Over time, we want to build a business that can serve most Indian households across income groups profitably.

Q6. Where are you in your journey of assortment expansion and how far can you go? Does broader e-commerce fit into your medium/ long term plans?
Albinder: We are still early. Assortment expansion is one of our highest priorities, because it is the biggest driver of how often customers come back and how much of their wallet share they bring to us.
We are making good progress. For example, in Delhi NCR, our assortment has grown from about 80,000 SKUs in Q4FY26 to about 100,000 today. We are expanding in two directions:
● Deeper: more choice within existing categories - more brands, sizes and price points.
● Wider: categories we don't carry yet.
Wider is harder. Every new category comes with its own supply chain problem. Large appliances need different storage and handling, fragile and high-value items need different packaging and security, and some categories have entirely different sourcing and returns. For each one, we have to figure out how much inventory to hold and where, how it reaches the customer, and whether we can do all that profitably.

On e-commerce, we don't think the line between quick commerce and e-commerce will mean much over time. For most purchases, if price and choice are similar, customers prefer to get things sooner. Demand is not the question. The question is whether you can build a supply chain that serves that demand reliably and profitably. That is the problem we have been solving. We want to bring most of what a household buys within 10 minutes.
Q7. Can private labels help improve margins further? Why does Blinkit not have a private label play?
Albinder: A private label has to pass one of two tests - either it fills a gap and brings incremental demand to the platform, or it improves the economics of demand we already serve, after accounting for everything it takes to build and market the private label. We have evaluated both and believe it doesn’t pass either of these tests.

The private label case rests on building something genuinely differentiated - a product customers choose for its quality, story-telling or design. That means building a brand, not just putting our name on a product - and involves continuous product development, manufacturing development, quality control, inventory management across a full portfolio of SKUs, sampling and marketing to drive trial and repeat. We believe brands will build these capabilities better and more efficiently than us as these would not be within our core circle of competence.
The exception is where deeper supply-chain control itself creates value. Fruits and vegetables are the clearest case - and Hyperpure already gives Blinkit that benefit through sourcing and quality control, without a separate consumer-facing brand.
Blinkit is the distribution and discovery platform for thousands of brands, many of them emerging. The shelf space and visibility we would spend marketing an own label can instead help other brands grow on our fair and neutral platform. This also allows us to earn advertising revenue as the brands grow. We don’t want to become both the platform and a competitor to the brands on the platform. We would rather avoid that conflict unless the growth or margin case for owning the label is clearly compelling.

Q8. The case for quick commerce in smaller cities is not very well established. Why are you so bullish on it?
Albinder: The skepticism usually rests on three assumptions - incomes are lower, basket is smaller, and density is too thin for the economics to work. Our data so far says the first is true but matters less than people expect. Data contradicts the other two.
Demand is there in these cities but has been chronically underserved. Organised retail could have served this demand with greater width of selection and better pricing but it never never fully developed in these cities. As a result, a lot of what we stock and sell is either not available locally or takes days to arrive through alternative channels like e-commerce. By making this assortment accessible within minutes, we create new demand and new behaviors for customers in these cities.
Three data points tell us this is real -
● Ramp: New stores in these cities reach 1,000 orders per day in similar time as new stores in metros (sometimes even faster).
● Basket: NAOVs are within 85-90% of metros, with baskets also containing categories that we did not expect - such as premium beverages, branded diapers, gaming consoles etc.
● Retention: Customer retention in these cities is comparable to that in the metros.

● Retention: Customer retention in these cities is comparable to that in the metros.
We also think building the supply to these cities is the harder part and something which will be a moat for us in the future. For many products we had to build first-mile capability, picking directly from brand warehouses into our mother warehouses that feed these cities.
We do not expect every small city to look like a metro. Some will stay subscale, and we will be disciplined about where we expand. But wherever we have built supply, demand has shown up faster and deeper than we had anticipated. In metros, we usually compete for a market that already exists. In smaller cities, we are building the market and the supply. That is why we are bullish.
Q9. Store addition seems to have accelerated with 308 net new stores in Q2FY27 taking the total to 2,751 stores. You seem comfortably on track on your guidance of 3,000 stores by March 2027. What’s the next milestone on this front?
Akshant: We now expect to cross 3,500 stores by March 2027, and our current plans point to about 5,000 stores by March 2028.
Two things give us the confidence to move faster than before -
1) New bets are working. Stores in smaller cities and stores built around newer categories are on the right margin and payback trajectory. Together, these will make up the bulk of the expansion.

2) We have a clearer read on competition. Across our more contested markets, new stores are clearing our return thresholds even at today's level of competitive intensity.
Our cash balance and profits from both food delivery and quick commerce businesses, also let us fund this pace of growth comfortably.
Q10. How does this acceleration impact the margins in the near-term and the NOV growth guidance of 60% CAGR over the next 3 years?
Akshant: We expect Adjusted EBITDA margins to keep improving through this expansion. New stores weigh on margins (and more so on Contribution) in their early months, but we expect the improvement in our more mature stores and cities to more than offset that.
That said, we don't manage this business for near-term margins. What matters more is evidence that the business can reach steady-state margins, and that evidence keeps getting stronger.
● Our mature cities already operate at over 5% Adjusted EBITDA margin.
● Cities contributing about 96% of our NOV are Contribution positive, and those contributing about 70% are Adjusted EBITDA positive. The progress is broad-based, not limited to a few cities.

● Cities contributing about 96% of our NOV are Contribution positive, and those contributing about 70% are Adjusted EBITDA positive. The progress is broad-based, not limited to a few cities.
On growth, NOV growth has moderated over the last three quarters to about 79% YoY in Q2FY27, mainly because we are now comparing against a much larger base. With more stores going live and ramping up over the next few quarters, we expect growth to pick up from here.
Over the longer term, we are two quarters into the three-year period covered by our 60% CAGR guidance. We are tracking ahead of it so far, but it is too early to revise it upwards.
Q11. In Jan 2026, you had given guidance of District Adjusted EBITDA break-even in 4-6 quarters. 3 quarters in, are we on track?
Akshant: Yes. We are getting there while growing faster than we expected when we gave that guidance. NOV growth is trending at 50%+ YoY, well ahead of the 30%+ CAGR built into our FY30 plan. We also remain on track towards our earlier guidance of INR 28,000 crore NOV (US$ 3 billion) and INR 1,400 crore (US$ 150 million) Adjusted EBITDA by FY30.

As Deepinder noted earlier, agentic commerce could disrupt parts of this business over time, and we are building with that in mind. A large part of durability in this business will come from building physical infrastructure and operations which deliver a differentiated customer experience. Like we mentioned earlier, where infrastructure becomes the product.
Q12. What is new and exciting at Hyperpure?
Akshant: Hyperpure now serves about 85,000 restaurants, up from 62,000 a year ago. We see three things driving that growth.
1. Speed. We now deliver within two hours in all major cities, and 25% of our orders already arrive within that window, and growing. This changes how restaurants procure. With a dependable two-hour option, they no longer need to plan and store large quantities of perishables, and we think that will steadily shift more of their purchasing to us.
2. Formalisation. Most restaurants still buy through mandis and wholesalers, often in cash. That is changing as food safety and other compliance requirements tighten and operators look for consistent quality. Every Hyperpure order is fully invoiced and traceable, which makes us a natural choice as restaurants move to organised supply.

3. Going beyond ingredients. We are becoming a broader supply chain partner for food businesses. We provide 3PL services to some of India's largest pan-India restaurant brands, and we now help restaurants set up complete kitchens, including equipment we source directly, some of it imported. Once a restaurant sets up its kitchen with us, we often go on to supply it with ingredients as well.
We compete with incumbent wholesalers and other B2B platforms that often compete on price alone. We don't try to be the cheapest. We compete on reliability, speed and quality, which is what restaurants value once they have tried us.
Q13. Can you share an update on the cash balance as at the end of Q2FY27?
Akshant: Cash balance declined by INR 1,813 crore during the quarter to end at INR 16,475 crore as at the end of Q2FY27. The main driver was a seasonal increase in net working capital (NWC) -
● In quick commerce, we built inventory ahead of the festive season.
● In food delivery, quarter-end fell at a point in the weekly restaurant settlement cycle that temporarily lowered payables.
‘Other Items’ declined largely due to -
● marked-to-market movements in the value of debt and other securities held by us. These are accounting movements, not realised losses. We hold these instruments to maturity.
● tax payout for the quarter. The previous quarter had the benefit of a tax refund.

In the letter below, we address the key questions that we think investors might have. Please refer to Annexure A for the key financial and operating metrics data.
Q1. How was the business performance in Q1FY27?
Akshant: Key takeaways from Q1FY27 business performance are as follows -
At a consolidated level, B2C NOV grew 54% YoY to INR 31,120 crore.
Adjusted Revenue grew 173% YoY (17% QoQ) to INR 20,648 crore. Note: like-for-like growth was 66% YoY - the difference reflects the business model shift to inventory ownership in quick commerce.
Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA grew 223% YoY (29% QoQ) to INR 555 crore.
Food delivery (Zomato) - NOV growth reached 20%+ YoY (INR 10,769 crore), after four consecutive quarters of acceleration. GOV YoY growth was a few percentage points higher (sunsetting this metric disclosure from this quarter onwards as NOV more accurately reflects underlying performance). Adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 5.6% of NOV, resulting in INR 606 crore of profit (34% YoY growth).

Quick commerce (Blinkit) - NOV grew 86% YoY to INR 17,132 crore with QoQ growth at 19%. 200 net new stores were added, taking the total count to 2,443. Adjusted EBITDA improved for the fifth consecutive quarter to 0.6% of NOV, resulting in INR 102 crore profit (as compared to INR 162 crore loss last year).
Going-out (District) - NOV growth accelerated to 60% YoY (18% QoQ) to INR 3,218 crore. Adjusted EBITDA margin improved to -2.0% of NOV from -2.7% last year resulting in a loss of INR 65 crore.
Hyperpure - Revenue grew 27% YoY (LFL) and 6% QoQ to INR 1,034 crore. Adjusted EBITDA margin improved to 0.6% from -0.8% last year, resulting in INR 6 crore profit (as compared to INR 18 crore loss last year).
Others (Bistro, Nugget) - Adjusted Revenue grew to INR 95 crore as compared to INR 4 crore last year. Adjusted EBITDA losses increased from INR 45 crore to INR 94 crore, reflecting incremental investments as we scale both initiatives.
Q2. Adjusted EBITDA margins in food delivery are approaching the upper end of your steady state guidance of 5-6% of NOV. And at the same time NOV growth continues to accelerate. At what point does the business start trading margin for growth, or does it not have to?

Q2. Adjusted EBITDA margins in food delivery are approaching the upper end of your steady state guidance of 5-6% of NOV. And at the same time NOV growth continues to accelerate. At what point does the business start trading margin for growth, or does it not have to?
Deepinder: We don't think about it as a trade-off. If we're doing our job well, growth and margins should compound together - because growth in this business comes from making the platform more useful to more people, which drives frequency, which drives density, which drives efficiency. The flywheel doesn't ask you to choose.
If there comes a point where we have to spend margin to grow, we will - without hesitation. We have always prioritised long-term market expansion over short-term margin. But right now, we don’t need to make any trade-off. The business is growing because it's getting better, not because we're buying growth. And when growth comes from the product getting better, margins tend to take care of themselves.
Q3. What has been the impact so far of Toing and Ownly on your business?

Q3. What has been the impact so far of Toing and Ownly on your business?
Deepinder: The impact has been limited. These platforms are offering the same restaurants, similar or longer delivery times, and lower menu prices funded by lower commissions and delivery fee - making the revenue gap even more unsustainable. There's no new use case being unlocked here. The customer traction is purely price-driven, and price-driven traction without structural economics tends to resolve itself.
We've responded where needed and we'll adapt if something changes. But we're not spending much energy on this.
What we are spending energy on is Bistro - which is our answer to the question these platforms are pretending to solve. If you want to make food delivery work at INR 50-150 price points, you can't do it without supply chain innovation. We're rethinking kitchen operations from first principles here - designing custom equipment, workflows, and automation purpose-built for high-volume, limited-menu formats. This isn't a restaurant. It's closer to a food manufacturing system optimised for freshness, speed, and consistency. It's a different segment, a different occasion, and a genuinely new market.
Q4. NOV growth has accelerated meaningfully (19% QoQ vs 8% in Q4FY26). Other than the seasonality factor you had mentioned last time, did anything else change?

Q4. NOV growth has accelerated meaningfully (19% QoQ vs 8% in Q4FY26). Other than the seasonality factor you had mentioned last time, did anything else change?
Albinder: It was largely seasonality and the NOV growth was on expected lines. We continue to focus our efforts on our three pillars of long-term growth - assortment expansion, geographical expansion, and demand densification. This quarter, we continued to make progress on assortment expansion in the top eight cities and geographic expansion in the next 30. Going forward, premiumisation through launch of ‘gourmet’ stores in select locations in top eight cities will also contribute to assortment expansion on the platform. These gourmet stores offer our customers the ability to buy curated premium brands across categories.
As these efforts compound over time, we expect NOV growth to remain robust.
Q5. Blinkit seems to be increasingly becoming more capital intensive with significant capex and net working capital. What's the framework for evaluating whether this level of investment is justified?

Q5. Blinkit seems to be increasingly becoming more capital intensive with significant capex and net working capital. What's the framework for evaluating whether this level of investment is justified?
Akshant: Quick commerce is not asset-light, unlike our other businesses. Today, we operate about 19 million sqft. of store and warehousing space across 300+ cities. We've invested ~INR 3,000 crore capex over the past four years to build this network, and as we continue to expand, the investments will continue. This is the most critical building block of our business and also our biggest differentiator.
As far as working capital is concerned, it is largely driven by inventory ownership - a business model choice we've made deliberately because it makes the business more durable in the long term. As at the end of Q1FY27, our net working capital is INR 2,545 crore (about ~14 days of Q1FY27 annualized NOV).
Our confidence in continuing to invest in capex and NWC is driven by expected ROCE. The math keeps evolving as we learn more about the business, but as long as a healthy ROCE remains in sight, we will continue to invest.

Our confidence in continuing to invest in capex and NWC is driven by expected ROCE. The math keeps evolving as we learn more about the business, but as long as a healthy ROCE remains in sight, we will continue to invest.
About a year ago, in our Q1FY26 letter, we shared our ROCE framework as we moved to the inventory model. Having completed a full year as a 1P business, we now have real operating data to refine those assumptions. Following is what we believe to be steady state assumptions, at this point -
● Capex per store (including warehousing): INR 2.5 crore (vs 1 crore earlier), reflecting larger store sizes, assortment expansion, and technology investments in warehousing ● Net working capital: 12 days of NOV, or 3.3% (vs 18 days / 5% earlier) ● NOV per day, per store: INR 11 lakh (vs INR 7 lakh earlier), driven by larger store sizes and more efficient warehousing ● EBIT margin: 4% of NOV (same as earlier); driven by 6% Adjusted EBITDA margin (higher end of our earlier guidance of 5-6%)
The math: INR 2.5 crore capex against INR 40 crore annual NOV per store (= INR 11 lakh * 365) implies 6.3% of NOV in capex. Add 3.3% for net working capital, and total capital employed is 9.6% of NOV. At 4% EBIT margin, that implies pre-tax ROCE of 41.7% (= 4/9.6).
These numbers will evolve as the business evolves.

These numbers will evolve as the business evolves.
Q6. It’s been a year since the transition to the 1P model. What has been your experience with inventory losses (which are generally a big concern in 1P businesses)?
Akshant: Inventory losses for us are about 1.8% of NOV right now, which include losses on account of expiry, shrinkage, damage, loss in transit or pilferage. A large part of these losses are driven by perishable products (including fruits and vegetables) which is an important and large category for us in the quick commerce business.
We believe this is a great start and we will continue to optimize them with better replenishment planning and supply chain efficiencies.
The inventory losses are part of COGS (cost of goods sold) and hence the reported Gross Profit is net of inventory losses.
Q7. Any impact of the fuel and raw material price inflation on the business? Any supply side challenges from brands that can impact growth in the near term?
Albinder: No, we are not seeing any visible impact as of now. Input costs across select raw materials are beginning to witness some inflationary pressure but that has not impacted production volumes or supply from brands so far.
Q8. Any change in how you are responding to competitive tactics?

Q8. Any change in how you are responding to competitive tactics?
Albinder: No - competitive intensity remains high but has become more predictable. Our focus on long-term growth vectors remains unique in the market - we're the only player simultaneously investing in assortment depth, geographic expansion, and supply chain infrastructure while competitors generally remain focused primarily on pricing. Pricing-led growth requires sustained cash burn, and leads QC companies into a systemic trap they can’t easily walk out of - that is visible in multiple QC players struggling to balance both growth and profitability. This is different from traditional e-commerce, where discounting can be weaned off gradually, without hurting the business (much).
Infrastructure-led growth, on the other hand, builds operating leverage - each new store, each new category, each new city adds capacity that serves more customers at lower marginal cost. That's why we can grow rapidly and improve profitability at the same time.
Akshant: The most critical signal of how we're doing against competition is customer retention. If customers are staying and spending more despite aggressive pricing from competitors, the business is working. Here's what the data shows -

Akshant: The most critical signal of how we're doing against competition is customer retention. If customers are staying and spending more despite aggressive pricing from competitors, the business is working. Here's what the data shows -
● Q4 retention (% of customers placing at least 1 order in the 4th quarter after acquisition): average across all cohorts is 46%, with every successive cohort improving - the most recent cohort (Q1FY26) is at 50% ● Retention improves with time - Q8 retention at 48%, Q12 at 49% - most recent cohorts that have completed Q8 and Q12 are even higher at 52% each ● NOV retention compounds even faster - Q4 at 150%, Q8 at 215%, Q12 at 279% average retention for all cohorts. In other words, a cohort of customers is spending nearly 3x with us three years after acquisition than they did in their first quarter
Q9. Going-out grew 60% YoY this quarter versus your earlier long-term guidance of 30%+. Is the $3 billion NOV by FY30 target conservative, or is Q1 growth inflated by seasonality?

Q9. Going-out grew 60% YoY this quarter versus your earlier long-term guidance of 30%+. Is the $3 billion NOV by FY30 target conservative, or is Q1 growth inflated by seasonality?
Deepinder: IPL was in Q1 last year as well - so the 60% YoY isn't a seasonality artifact. The acceleration is real, driven by the platform coming together as a unified multi-use-case app and the compounding effects of that breadth on customer engagement and frequency. Today, District generates visibility and business for 45,000+ restaurants, 5,000+ movie screens, 6,000+ retail stores, 7,500+ events (music concerts, comedy shows, sports events, etc) and 2,000+ activity outlets (theme parks, sports facilities, kids play areas etc).
That said, as we also mentioned last time, this is an inherently lumpy business - movies depend on the release calendar, events are seasonal, and a single quarter doesn't make a trend. If we continue executing well and the market develops as we expect, there could be upside to the target but it’s too early to tell.
Q10. Can you give us an update on the ‘Others’ segment - what all gets included in it and what is driving the increase in losses?

Q10. Can you give us an update on the ‘Others’ segment - what all gets included in it and what is driving the increase in losses?
Akshant: The Others segment includes our key new initiatives — Bistro, Nugget, and Greening India — as well as, from Q1FY27 onwards, our community initiatives (Blinkit ambulance service, Feeding India) which are now being consolidated under a wholly owned section 8 (i.e. not for profit) subsidiary, Eternal General Services Foundation.
The QoQ increase this quarter was largely driven by R&D investments in Nugget as we scale our AI product capabilities.
Think of this segment as the cost of experimentation - finding potential new businesses for Eternal beyond the four that exist today. We'll invest meaningfully but with discipline, and we won't hesitate to shut things down if they don't show promise within a reasonable timeframe. On the other hand, if something shows real promise, we won't hesitate to invest more aggressively. The spend in this segment will be driven by what we're seeing in the data and hearing from our customers, not by a pre-determined budget.
Q11. Are there any parts of the employee or technology cost that are capitalised?
Akshant: No, everything is expensed and reported in the P&L above Adjusted EBITDA.
Q12. Can you share an update on the cash balance as at the end of Q1FY27?

Q12. Can you share an update on the cash balance as at the end of Q1FY27?
Akshant: Cash balance increased by INR 316 crore QoQ to INR 18,288 crore. See the table below for more details. Capex and net working capital changes have been explained in Q5 above. The only other meaningful change is in ‘Other items’ which is due to the marked-to-market movements in the value of debt and other securities held by us, and also due to tax refunds received this quarter.
